content.title: About
content.content: Adobo is a classic Filipino dish made from meat (usually chicken or pork) marinated in a mixture of soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, bay leaf, and spices, then simmered until tender. The “with rice” version is served alongside steamed white rice, creating a hearty and balanced meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “adobo” comes from the Spanish word “adobo,” meaning “marinade.”
Traditional recipes use vinegar to help preserve meat in the hot Philippine climate.
There are many regional variations, ranging from sweet with added sugar to spicy with chili.
Adobo is often considered the national dish of the Philippines and is served at celebrations and family gatherings.
Pairing adobo with rice makes the dish a complete source of protein and carbohydrates.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat in adobo provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: The fermentation of vinegar supports the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Traditional recipes do not include added sugar, making the dish suitable for moderate carbohydrate intake.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and soy sauce supply vitamins B6 and B12, which aid nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides iron, zinc, and magnesium, important for immunity and energy production.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce can be very salty; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy products.

items.title: Acidity of vinegar
items.content: Large amounts of vinegar may irritate the stomach in those with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Meat fat content
items.content: Using fatty cuts can make the dish calorie‑dense; opting for leaner pieces is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve adobo hot, sliced into pieces and drizzled with its sauce. Rice can be eaten plain or mixed with the sauce for extra flavor. The dish is often accompanied by fresh vegetables or pickled cucumbers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked adobo in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.
